_about: CLAUDE.md 5ft (30 X 2026): hand-written notes for properties the Graph radar found in our developer tenant before Microsoft's $metadata knew them. Key: type|property. basis: microsoft = Microsoft described the feature (Message Center, Learn), article = a community article names it, name = our reading of the property's name only (nothing published yet). uses: what an admin could do with it - our suggestion, never Microsoft's text. articles: checked by hand on the day in 'checked'; rel names-it = the article names this property, feature = the article describes the feature, not the property. Author: Piotr Wisniewski. 5fy (31 X 2026, owner: 'show a full example of use - the community describes it'): optional values (sub-property, type, accepted values, what, src = the article key), examples (title, what, method, uri, scopes, body, tested, src), caveats; an article with unread: true was named by the owner or a search but our reader could not open it. Notes written by the morning routine live in site/data/graph-radar-notes.json, same shape (tools/radar_todo.py check).

passwordAuthenticationMethodConfiguratio.title: Password change after a secure sign-in
passwordAuthenticationMethodConfiguratio.what: Lets users change their password in My Sign-Ins after signing in with a strong credential (passkey, FIDO2 security key, Windows Hello for Business), without typing the current password and without SSPR. Off by default; Microsoft rolls it out worldwide in October and November 2026 (MC1437671). Jan Bakker (30/10/2026): not in the Entra admin center yet - Graph is the only way to turn it on - and it applies to the whole tenant, it cannot be scoped to users or groups.
uses: Users who sign in passwordless but still keep a password for an old app or VPN can rotate it themselves, without a help desk call
It applies to the whole tenant (no user or group scope) - try it in a test tenant first and tell the help desk before you switch it on
Pair it with an authentication strength that requires phishing-resistant MFA, so only a strong sign-in opens the password change
Turning it on needs Policy.ReadWrite.AuthenticationMethod and at least the Authentication Policy Administrator role (Jan Bakker)
In a tenant review: off means users who forgot their password still go through SSPR or the help desk

articles.title: MC1437671 - Microsoft Entra: Allow password change after secure sign-in with My Sign-Ins
articles.says: Lets users who signed in with a passkey, FIDO2 key or Windows Hello for Business set a new password in My Sign-Ins without knowing the current one and without SSPR; it is off by default, tenant-wide only (no per-user or per-group scoping), and must be turned on by an admin. General availability (worldwide and GCC) starts at the end of October 2026 and should finish by the end of November 2026 (updated 9 Oct 2026).

articles.title: Allow password change after secure sign-in
articles.says: The setting is not in the Entra admin center yet, so you enable it by sending a PATCH to the beta Password authentication method configuration with allowPasswordChangeAfterSecureSignIn=true (Graph Explorer or Invoke-MgGraphRequest, Policy.ReadWrite.AuthenticationMethod, at least Authentication Policy Administrator). It applies to the whole tenant, and the rollout runs from late October to the end of November 2026.
articles.tested: Sent the PATCH from Graph Explorer and got a successful response (shown in a screenshot); the user experience itself was not tested.

articles.title: Microsoft Entra: Passwordless password change in My Sign-Ins

defaultUserRolePermissions|allowedToCrea.title: Users can register agent identity blueprints
defaultUserRolePermissions|allowedToCrea.what: The switch behind 'Users can register agent identity blueprints' in Default user role permissions of the authorization policy. It is separate from 'Users can register applications', so blocking app registrations does not block blueprints. Three community articles describe it; Microsoft has not put it in $metadata yet.
uses: Set it to false so that only admins (or apps with AgentIdentityBlueprint.Create) create agent identity blueprints - the same reason most tenants block app registrations
Add it to the tenant baseline next to allowedToCreateApps, allowedToCreateTenants and allowedToCreateSecurityGroups
Audit: read it before 04/11/2026, the date from which Jan Bakker writes that every user without a role can create blueprints unless it is off
PATCH /policies/authorizationPolicy/authorizationPolicy with Policy.ReadWrite.Authorization (beta only for now)

articles.title: Prevent users from creating new agent identity blueprints
articles.says: From 4 November 2026, every user without an Entra role can create agent identity blueprints unless an admin turns this off, either in Entra admin center > Users > User settings > 'Users can register agent identity blueprints' = No, or by sending a PATCH to beta authorizationPolicy with allowedToCreateAgentIdentityBlueprints=false (Policy.ReadWrite.Authorization). The property is only on the beta endpoint for now (based on MC1506733).

articles.title: Microsoft Entra Lets Users Create Agent Blueprints by Default
articles.says: The new setting 'Users can create agent blueprints' is on by default and lives in authorizationPolicy as allowedToCreateAgentIdentityBlueprints, which is beta-only, undocumented and may still be renamed. It takes effect as the rollout reaches each tenant, from 4 November to late November 2026, and you can switch it off in User settings or through a beta PATCH; users who still need to create blueprints can be given the Agent ID Developer role.
articles.tested: The toggle showed up in the author's tenant only after a hard refresh (Ctrl+F5); the author suggests a two-account test but gives no result for it.

articles.title: Entra Disable User Creation of Agent Identity Blueprints
articles.says: 'Users can register agent identity blueprints' is on by default. The post turns it off with Microsoft Graph PowerShell by sending a PATCH to beta policies/authorizationPolicy/authorizationPolicy that sets defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateAgentIdentityBlueprints=$false.
articles.tested: Read defaultUserRolePermissions with a GET, sent the PATCH, then read it again; the screenshots show the setting off ('Now it's turned off').

voiceAuthenticationMethodConfiguration|i.title: Custom greeting in voice-call MFA
voiceAuthenticationMethodConfiguration|i.what: Whether voice-call MFA plays the tenant's own greeting. Microsoft retired custom greetings in voice call authentication on 28/02/2026 (MC1219798): calls now play Microsoft's default recording. Most likely the switch of the retired feature, still returned by the service.
uses: Check it is false - after the retirement a custom greeting is no longer played
Audit evidence: true shows the tenant still had custom greetings configured before the retirement
Remove the greeting from your MFA user guides and help desk scripts

articles.title: MC1219798 - Custom greetings in voice call authentication will retire on Feb 28, 2026
articles.says: Custom greetings for voice call MFA retire on 28 February 2026; after that, voice call authentication uses Microsoft's default recordings. The retirement happens automatically, so admins only need to prepare users.

authenticationMethodsPolicy|optOutSettin.title: Opt out of the automatic passkey switch-on
authenticationMethodsPolicy|optOutSettin.what: A tenant-wide opt-out on the authentication methods policy. Its one known setting, passkeyDynamicMigration = true, keeps the tenant out of Microsoft's automatic passkey enablement and the Microsoft-managed passkey registration campaign that come with the retirement of Microsoft-provided SMS and voice (changes from 1 September 2026). Microsoft documents it in the Entra article on the SMS and voice retirement, not in the Graph reference.
uses: Delay the automatic passkey enablement while you configure a telephony provider or move users to another method
Check it in every tenant you manage: null = no opt-out was set
Plan for the end: from 1 February 2027 (1 July 2027 for Global Administrators and external users) the retirement applies whatever this says

articles.title: Passkeys by default and retirement of Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication (section: Temporarily opt out of the automatic passkey enablement)
articles.says: Says that setting optOutSettings.passkeyDynamicMigration to true with a PATCH to the beta authenticationmethodspolicy endpoint temporarily excludes the tenant from the automatic passkey enablement and Registration Campaign rollout (1 Sep 2026 to 1 Feb 2027). It requires Policy.ReadWrite.AuthenticationMethod and does not stop the retirement enforcement dates.

articles.title: 自動パスキー有効化を一時的にオプトアウトする手順 (Steps to temporarily opt out of automatic passkey enablement)
articles.by: Hasegawa, Microsoft Japan Azure & Identity support team (jpazureid blog)
articles.says: Gives step-by-step Graph PowerShell commands to read optOutSettings with a GET and set passkeyDynamicMigration to true with a PATCH on /beta/policies/authenticationmethodspolicy. Notes that the GET returns nothing when no opt-out has been set, and that Global Administrator, or Cloud Application Administrator plus Authentication Policy Administrator, is needed.
articles.tested: GET before (empty when not set), PATCH, GET after to confirm; a screenshot of the PowerShell session is included

articles.title: How to Disable Passkey Prompts and Delay Enforcement in Microsoft 365
articles.says: Shows an Invoke-MgGraphRequest PATCH to /beta/policies/authenticationMethodsPolicy with optOutSettings.passkeyDynamicMigration = $true, then a GET to check the value. Stresses that true means the tenant is opting OUT and that the opt-out does not change the retirement dates.

articles.title: SAW Authentication Assessment Toolkit - rule AUTH006 'Passkey Dynamic Migration Not Opted Out'
articles.says: An assessment rule that flags tenants that have not set authenticationMethodsPolicy.optOutSettings.passkeyDynamicMigration (beta only). It explains that true opts the tenant out of the 1 Sep 2026 automatic enablement but not out of the 1 Feb 2027 retirement.
articles.tested: The commit message says the author checked the absent, false and true states manually and ran the full sample-data pipeline

values.name: optOutSettings.passkeyDynamicMigration
values.accepted: true = opted OUT of the automatic passkey enablement and registration campaign; false or absent = not opted out
values.what: The name reads backwards: true means you opted out. GET returns optOutSettings as null until someone sets it.

examples.title: Opt the tenant out of the automatic passkey switch-on
examples.what: Microsoft's own request from the SMS and voice retirement article. Read the policy before and after.
examples.tested: Microsoft's documented request; Microsoft Japan's identity support blog shows the GET before and after; Kenneth van Surksum's toolkit checks absent / false / true.

caveats: Beta only, and temporary: from 1 February 2027 (1 July 2027 for Global Administrators and external users) the passkey migration and enforcement apply regardless of this setting - there is no opt-out from the retirement itself.
Needs Policy.ReadWrite.AuthenticationMethod; Microsoft Japan's blog names Global Administrator, or Cloud Application Administrator together with Authentication Policy Administrator.

x509CertificateAuthenticationMethodConfi.title: CRL validation of certificate-based authentication
x509CertificateAuthenticationMethodConfi.what: How Entra checks certificate revocation lists (CRL) for certificate-based authentication. Microsoft documents it in Graph v1.0 (x509CertificateCrlValidationConfiguration); only the beta $metadata lacks it.
uses: Check that CRL validation is required for your certificate authorities - an unchecked CRL accepts revoked certificates
List the exempted CAs and ask why each one is exempt
Use the v1.0 endpoint for scripts: it is documented there

articles.title: x509CertificateCrlValidationConfiguration resource type (v1.0)
articles.says: This v1.0 resource decides whether certificate-based authentication fails when the issuing CA has no valid CRL distribution point. state can be disabled, enabled or unknownFutureValue, and exemptedCertificateAuthoritiesSubjectKeyIdentifiers lists the subject key identifiers (in hex) of CAs that are exempt from the check.

federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticatio.title: New authentication method: federated identity credential - who it applies to
federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticatio.what: The whole method configuration 'federatedIdentityCredential' is new: it is not in $metadata at all. includeTargets is the usual 'which users and groups' list every method has. Nothing published yet.
uses: Read which groups it targets in your tenant - a new sign-in method that appears enabled for 'all users' is worth knowing about
Watch for the MC post or Learn page that introduces the method
Compare with the other methods' includeTargets when you review the authentication methods policy

articles.title: ScubaGear sample report (ScubaResults JSON) showing authenticationMethodConfigurations('FederatedIdentityCredential')
articles.says: A tenant export lists a method with id FederatedIdentityCredential and state disabled. Its includeTargets holds one entry: targetType group, id all_users, isRegistrationRequired false, allowedProfiles [].
articles.tested: GET only, as part of a ScubaGear run; state disabled, includeTargets = all_users

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365wp: authentication_methods_policy.go strips federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticationMethodConfiguration
articles.says: The provider code removes entries of type federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticationMethodConfiguration from the authentication methods policy it reads, with a comment that the type has 'not yet been documented anywhere'.

federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticatio.title: New authentication method: federated identity credential - profiles
federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticatio.what: Profiles of the new, unpublished 'federatedIdentityCredential' authentication method; the name suggests several configurations of the method (for example per external identity provider). Nothing published yet.
uses: Read it to see whether your tenant has a profile already
Keep it on the watch list with includeTargets of the same method

articles.title: ScubaGear sample report (ScubaResults JSON) showing FederatedIdentityCredential profiles
articles.says: Shows Profiles as an empty array on the FederatedIdentityCredential method, with its own @odata.context pointing to .../authenticationMethodConfigurations('FederatedIdentityCredential')/.../profiles.
articles.tested: GET only; profiles = []

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365wp: authentication_methods_policy.go strips federatedIdentityCredentialAuthenticationMethodConfiguration
articles.says: The whole federatedIdentityCredential method configuration, profiles included, is dropped by the provider because the type is not documented.

crossTenantAccessPolicy|applyDefaultsToD.title: Apply cross-tenant defaults to domain-based organizations
crossTenantAccessPolicy|applyDefaultsToD.what: A switch on the cross-tenant access policy. The name says the default settings would also apply to external organizations identified by domain rather than by tenant ID. Nothing published yet.
uses: Read it before you change the default cross-tenant settings - it may widen what the defaults cover
Watch for the documentation before relying on it in B2B designs

articles.title: Tenant Management Framework - Export-TmfCrossTenantAccessDefaultSetting.ps1 / Export-TmfCrossTenantAccessPartnerSetting.ps1
articles.says: The export function removes applyDefaultsToDomainBasedOrganizations from the retrieved settings, together with system fields such as policyTenantId, migrationStatus, version and lastModifiedDateTime, so the property is never exported.

articles.title: IntuneLab EntraBackup - crossTenantAccessPolicy.json
articles.says: A backup of the crossTenantAccessPolicy object shows applyDefaultsToDomainBasedOrganizations: false.
articles.tested: GET only (backup export); value false

crossTenantAccessPolicyInboundTrust|isCo.title: Trust a compliant network from another tenant
crossTenantAccessPolicyInboundTrust|isCo.what: Whether your Conditional Access accepts the 'compliant network' claim (Global Secure Access) of users from another Entra organization, like it can accept their MFA or compliant device. Microsoft describes it on the beta Learn page of crossTenantAccessPolicyInboundTrust; the $metadata lacks it.
uses: Partners who use Global Secure Access: accept their compliant network so your 'require compliant network' policy does not block them
Review it next to isMfaAccepted and isCompliantDeviceAccepted in the default and partner configurations
Keep it false for partners you do not know well

articles.title: crossTenantAccessPolicyInboundTrust resource type (beta)
articles.says: In the beta inbound trust settings of cross-tenant access policy, isCompliantNetworkAccepted is a Boolean that says whether a compliant network claim from external Entra organizations is trusted. It sits alongside isMfaAccepted, isCompliantDeviceAccepted and isHybridAzureADJoinedDeviceAccepted.

crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationDefa.title: Cross-cloud meetings in the default cross-tenant settings
crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationDefa.what: A block in the default cross-tenant access settings. The name matches Teams cross-cloud meetings (meeting people in other Microsoft 365 clouds, for example GCC High or 21Vianet), which Microsoft describes on Learn; the property itself is not named there.
uses: Read it if you meet organizations in another Microsoft cloud - the setting may decide whether those meetings work
Compare it with the Teams cross-cloud meeting settings described on Learn

articles.title: Meet with people in other Microsoft 365 cloud environments
articles.says: Teams cross-cloud meeting connections let users join meetings with an organization in another Microsoft 365 cloud (for example commercial and GCC) as authenticated participants without guest accounts. Each connection is built on Entra cross-tenant access settings, has its own Inbound and Outbound toggle in the Teams admin center, and must be configured by both organizations. The page does not name the Graph property; if the host tenant requires MFA, users can hit AADSTS90072 unless inbound MFA trust is configured.

articles.title: Get policyDeletableItem (beta) - example response for a deleted crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationPartner
articles.says: The example response for a deleted cross-tenant partner configuration includes crossCloudMeetingConfiguration with inboundAllowed null and outboundAllowed null. The property is not described.

articles.title: Configure cross-tenant synchronization using PowerShell or Microsoft Graph API (partner POST response)
articles.says: The example response after creating a partner configuration (POST to /policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/partners) includes crossCloudMeetingConfiguration {inboundAllowed: null, outboundAllowed: null}. The property is not described.

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365 api_docs.md - captured portal GET /policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/default
articles.says: A captured Entra portal request (GET /policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/default) shows crossCloudMeetingConfiguration with inboundAllowed false and outboundAllowed false on the default policy.
articles.tested: GET only (captured portal traffic); false/false

articles.title: Meet with people in other Microsoft 365 cloud environments
articles.says: Does not name the property. Explains that Teams cross-cloud meeting connections use organizations defined in Entra cross-tenant access settings, with Inbound and Outbound connection toggles per organization in the Teams admin center.

values.name: crossCloudMeetingConfiguration.inboundAllowed
values.what: Allowed for people and content coming in from other organizations. The portal's default policy: false / false.

values.name: crossCloudMeetingConfiguration.outboundAllowed
values.what: Allowed going out to other organizations. Partner entries in Microsoft's examples carry null.

caveats: Shown only in Microsoft's example responses (partner objects), never in a property table; nobody has published a PATCH.
The Teams article on meetings across Microsoft clouds describes the same inbound/outbound switches but does not name the property - the link is by name only.

crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationDefa.title: Protected content sharing in the default cross-tenant settings
crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationDefa.what: A block in the default cross-tenant access settings. The name points to sharing protected (encrypted, labelled) content with other organizations. Nothing published yet.
uses: Read it when partners cannot open your encrypted mail or labelled files
Keep it on the watch list with the Purview sensitivity label settings

articles.title: Get policyDeletableItem (beta) - example response for a deleted crossTenantAccessPolicyConfigurationPartner
articles.says: The example response for a deleted cross-tenant partner configuration includes protectedContentSharing with inboundAllowed null and outboundAllowed null. The property is not described.

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365 api_docs.md - captured portal GET /policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/default
articles.says: A captured Entra portal GET of the default cross-tenant policy shows protectedContentSharing with inboundAllowed true and outboundAllowed true.
articles.tested: GET only (captured portal traffic); true/true

values.name: protectedContentSharing.inboundAllowed
values.what: Allowed for people and content coming in from other organizations. The portal's default policy: true / true.

values.name: protectedContentSharing.outboundAllowed
values.what: Allowed going out to other organizations. Partner entries in Microsoft's examples carry null.

caveats: Shown only in Microsoft's example responses (partner objects), never in a property table; nobody has published a PATCH.

identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolic.title: Security defaults: which controls they enforce
identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolic.what: A list on the security defaults policy. The name says which controls security defaults enforce (for example MFA registration, blocking legacy authentication). Nothing published yet.
uses: Read it in tenants that run security defaults - it may show which protections are on
Watch it: a list of controls hints that security defaults may become configurable control by control

articles.title: IntuneCD - update/Entra/SecurityDefaults.py
articles.says: IntuneCD leaves controlTypes out of the compare and update of the security defaults policy, along with securityDefaultsUpsell, displayName and description.

articles.title: nodoc-ibiza-iam - security_defaults.yml (undocumented portal API /SecurityDefaults/Configuration)
articles.says: An OpenAPI spec of the undocumented portal endpoint /SecurityDefaults/Configuration lists controlTypes as a nullable array with example null, next to isEnabled and ignoreBaselineProtectionPolicies.

identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolic.title: Security defaults: automatic switch-on date
identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolic.what: Tells whether and when Microsoft will switch security defaults on by itself in this tenant: an action and a due date. CIPP alerts on it when security defaults are off and the action is autoEnable or autoEnabledNotify. Microsoft's Learn page describes the automatic enablement but does not name this property.
uses: Alert before Microsoft switches security defaults on in a tenant that relies on something else (CIPP does exactly this)
Read the due date in every managed tenant: action none = nothing planned
If the tenant should keep security defaults off, put Conditional Access or premium licensing in place before the date (Learn's conditions for automatic enablement)

articles.title: CIPP alert Get-CIPPAlertSecDefaultsUpsell.ps1
articles.says: The alert GETs /beta/policies/identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolicy. If isEnabled is false and securityDefaultsUpsell.action is autoEnable or autoEnabledNotify, it reports 'Security Defaults will be automatically enabled on {dueDateTime}'.

articles.title: IntuneCD - update/Entra/SecurityDefaults.py
articles.says: IntuneCD leaves securityDefaultsUpsell out of the compare and update of the security defaults policy.

articles.title: Security defaults in Microsoft Entra ID (section Enabling security defaults)
articles.says: Does not name the property. Says customers are periodically notified that security defaults will be automatically enabled if they have no Conditional Access policies, no premium licenses and no active legacy authentication clients.

values.name: securityDefaultsUpsell.action
values.what: CIPP treats autoEnable and autoEnabledNotify as 'will be switched on automatically'.

values.name: securityDefaultsUpsell.dueDateTime
values.what: The day Microsoft switches security defaults on; CIPP prints it as the enablement date.

examples.title: Check whether Microsoft will switch security defaults on (CIPP's test)
examples.what: Read the policy: isEnabled false and action autoEnable or autoEnabledNotify means security defaults will be switched on at dueDateTime.
examples.tested: The logic of CIPP's production alert (Get-CIPPAlertSecDefaultsUpsell).

caveats: Read-only as far as anyone shows - IntuneCD leaves it out of compare and update.
Our earlier reading (a prompt to move to Conditional Access) was wrong: the sources tie it to the automatic enablement of security defaults.

appManagementApplicationConfiguration|fe.title: App management policy: rules for federated identity credentials
appManagementApplicationConfiguration|fe.what: A new restriction in the tenant's app management policy (applicationRestrictions). The name says the policy can now govern federated identity credentials (workload identity federation, for example GitHub Actions or Kubernetes) on app registrations. Nothing published yet.
uses: When documented: allow federated credentials only from issuers you trust (your GitHub organization, your clusters)
Inventory today: list apps with federated credentials and their issuers - the restriction will act on them

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365 - scripts/powershell/applications/config/policy-comprehensive.json
articles.says: A tenant app management policy JSON lists applicationRestrictions.federatedIdentityCredentials as null, next to audiences, redirectUris and trustedSubjectNameAndIssuers (also null).

appManagementApplicationConfiguration|tr.title: App management policy: trusted certificate subjects and issuers
appManagementApplicationConfiguration|tr.what: A new restriction in the app management policy. The name says certificates on app registrations could be limited to trusted subject names and issuers - a step beyond the 'trusted certificate authorities' restriction Microsoft introduced in 2023. Nothing published for this property.
uses: When documented: accept app certificates only from your own CA and with expected subject names
Inventory today: which apps use certificates, from which issuers

articles.title: Introducing Trusted Certificate Authorities (public preview) in App management policy
articles.says: This November 2023 post announces a public preview of trusted certificate authority restrictions in app management policy: admins define trusted issuer chains (certificateBasedApplicationConfiguration) and then block app certificates from other issuers, including self-signed ones. It requires Workload ID premium, allows up to 5 trusted CAs per policy, and checks existing apps only when they rotate certificates. The post does not mention trustedSubjectNameAndIssuers by name.

articles.title: terraform-provider-microsoft365 - scripts/powershell/applications/config/policy-comprehensive.json
articles.says: Lists applicationRestrictions.trustedSubjectNameAndIssuers as null in a tenant app management policy JSON.

articles.title: Azure/ARO-HCP - dev-infrastructure/modules/entra/app.bicep and templates/geneva-identities.bicep (application property for SNI authentication)
articles.says: Sets a property with the same name on an application (Microsoft.Graph/applications@beta, not the policy) to [{authorityId, subjectName}] when SNI is used. The module describes it as 'Trusted subject name and issuer pairs for SNI authentication'.

articles.title: Azure/ARO-HCP - docs/ci/dev-mock-identities.md (historical note on SNI)
articles.says: Says an earlier setup configured SNI (trustedSubjectNameAndIssuers) on apps. That fails for self-signed certificates when the client sends the chain (AADSTS7000213) and caused a CI-wide auth outage, so the apps now use pinned keyCredentials.
articles.tested: Used in their CI: SNI sign-ins failed with AADSTS7000213 for self-signed certs sent with the chain

articles.title: Configure an App Registration in the Microsoft CORP tenant to trust certificates based on Subject Name + Issuer (Microsoft Q&A)
articles.by: Nick Andres (question), Sridevi Machavarapu (Microsoft External Staff, answer)
articles.says: Does not name the property. A Microsoft External Staff answer says trusting certificates by subject name and issuer is not supported for app registrations, and that no portal setting, Graph API parameter or tenant policy enables it.

appManagementServicePrincipalConfigurati.title: App management policy: credentials on service principals
appManagementServicePrincipalConfigurati.what: A new restriction for service principals (enterprise applications) in the app management policy. Nothing published yet.
uses: Inventory today: service principals that carry their own secrets or certificates - a common place for forgotten credentials
When documented: block new credentials on service principals the way the policy already can for app registrations

conditionalAccessPolicy|templateId.title: Conditional Access policy created from a template
conditionalAccessPolicy|templateId.what: The template a Conditional Access policy was created from. Documented in Graph v1.0; only the beta $metadata lacks it.
uses: Find the policies made from Microsoft's templates and compare them with the current template
Report how many of your policies are templates and how many are your own design

conditionalAccessPolicy|partialEnablemen.title: Conditional Access: partial enablement
conditionalAccessPolicy|partialEnablemen.what: The companion of a Conditional Access policy state partiallyEnabled, which the admin center shows as 'Staged rollout': the API refuses that state unless partialEnablementStrategy is set. Its format is not public - every published policy shows null, and the one write attempt published failed.
uses: When documented: roll a new policy out in stages instead of report-only followed by on for everyone
Read it now to see whether Microsoft-managed policies in your tenant already use it

articles.title: What is the Conditional Access Staged Rollout status?
articles.says: The portal has a new CA policy status 'Staged rollout' (state 'partiallyEnabled'), and Graph refuses that state unless partialEnablementStrategy is set. The author could not work out the property's format.
articles.tested: GET with $filter state eq 'partiallyEnabled' returned no policies; PATCH state=PartiallyEnabled failed with error 1211; adding PartialEnablementStrategy='Enabled' failed with schema errors

articles.title: Get conditionalAccessPolicy (beta) - example response
articles.says: The beta example response contains "partialEnablementStrategy": null. The property is not described. (Read from the docs source file in microsoft-graph-docs-contrib.)

articles.title: Create conditionalAccessPolicy (beta) - example responses
articles.says: Several beta create-policy example responses include "partialEnablementStrategy": null, but the page has no description of it. (Read from the docs source file.)

articles.title: Tutorial: Entra Internet Access via Microsoft Graph - example response
articles.says: A CA policy in the tutorial's example response includes "partialEnablementStrategy": null, with no explanation. (Read from the docs source file.)

articles.title: Conditional Access Policy Field Mapping (Graph beta)
articles.says: Lists it as a root field the API always adds with a default of null (String/null, 'Partial enablement config') and recommends treating it as read-only/computed.
articles.tested: 6 create-policy tests against beta: the field was added as null in every response

articles.title: CippCAPolicyBuilder.jsx (strips the key before re-deploying a policy)
articles.says: The CA policy builder removes the partialEnablementStrategy key along with other server-generated keys (id, templateId, deletedDateTime) when it processes a policy.

articles.title: DCToolbox.psm1 - CA policy JSON templates
articles.says: Its embedded CA policy JSON templates include "partialEnablementStrategy": null.

values.name: state
values.accepted: "partiallyEnabled" (portal: Staged rollout) - next to enabled, disabled, enabledForReportingButNotEnforced
values.what: Setting it alone fails: "1211: 'PartiallyEnabled' state requires PartialEnablementStrategy to be set".

values.name: partialEnablementStrategy
values.accepted: null in every published policy; the string "Enabled" was rejected with schema errors
values.what: Nobody has published a working value.

values.name: partialEnablementTargetRegions
values.what: A related property seen in the portal's validation request.

caveats: No working example exists - do not try it on a production policy.
CIPP strips it before redeploying a policy, and the Terraform provider treats it as read-only.

conditionalAccessConditionSet|times.title: Conditional Access condition: time (working hours)
conditionalAccessConditionSet|times.what: A time condition on a Conditional Access policy: the policy applies on the days and hours you set, or outside them. Microsoft has not documented it, but community admins set it through the beta API and tested it: a Block policy with the working hours excluded blocked every sign-in outside 08:00-16:00 and at the weekend, and let sign-ins inside the window through.
uses: Block sign-ins outside working hours for one group (contractors, shift staff, a pilot group) - start in report-only
Ask for MFA or a compliant device outside office hours instead of blocking
Always exclude the emergency access (break-glass) accounts - a time block can lock admins out at night
Supported today without this condition: switch a policy on and off on a schedule (Azure Automation runbook - Tony Redmond's article)

values.name: times.includeAllTimes
values.what: true + excludeDays: the policy applies all the time except the excluded window (Patyk's test: blocked outside Mon-Fri 07:00-15:00 UTC). false + includeDays: the policy applies only inside the window (Bradley's body).

values.name: times.includeDays / times.excludeDays
values.accepted: one window: daysOfWeek, timeZone, startTime, endTime, allDay
values.what: The days and hours the policy covers (include) or skips (exclude). Both articles set one of the two and send the other as null.

values.name: …Days.daysOfWeek
values.accepted: lowercase English day names: "monday" … "friday" in both articles
values.what: The days of the window.

values.name: …Days.timeZone
values.what: UTC has no summer time: 07:00-15:00 UTC is 08:00-16:00 in Poland in winter (CET) and 09:00-17:00 in summer (CEST).

values.name: …Days.startTime / …Days.endTime
values.what: Start and end of the window on each listed day.

values.name: …Days.allDay
values.what: true presumably means the whole day - no article tested it.

values.name: times.includeRange / times.excludeRange
values.accepted: timeZone, startDateTime, endDateTime (all null in the portal's code)
values.what: A date range (from - to). Daniel Bradley found the shape in the admin center's JavaScript; nobody has published a working range yet.

examples.title: A complete policy: block sign-ins outside working hours (report-only)
examples.what: Mon-Fri 08:00-16:00 Polish winter time (07:00-15:00 UTC) is allowed, everything else is blocked - nights and the whole weekend. Report-only first: read the sign-in logs, then switch state to "enabled".
examples.tested: The times block is Damian Patyk's, tested 17-21/02/2026 with a PATCH (allowed 14:47 UTC, blocked 15:18 UTC, blocked on Saturday). The rest is Microsoft's documented policy shape. We have not run this POST ourselves.

examples.title: Add the time condition to a policy you already have
examples.what: Damian Patyk's exact call: GET the policies, take the id, PATCH only conditions.times. A successful PATCH returns 204 No Content.
examples.tested: Tested by the author (Graph Explorer, February 2026).

examples.title: The other way round: the policy applies only inside the window
examples.what: Daniel Bradley's body: includeAllTimes false and includeDays Mon-Fri 09:00-17:00 UTC - the policy covers only those hours.
examples.tested: The author added it to a policy in Graph Explorer (January 2026); the admin center then showed a condition but listed every condition as "Not configured".

caveats: Undocumented and beta only - Microsoft may rename it, change it or switch it off without notice.
Only "UTC" is accepted. Move the hours twice a year (last Sunday of March and of October) or the window shifts by one hour.

The admin center does not show it: the policy lists every condition as "Not configured". The sign-in log names the policy that blocked, but its Conditions section is empty - write the reason in the policy's name.

Conditional Access is checked when a token is issued. Access tokens live 60-90 minutes, and with Continuous Access Evaluation (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint) up to 28 hours - a session started inside the window may go on after it closes. Neither article tested this.

articles.title: Configuring Time-based Conditional Access Policies
articles.says: Shows the PATCH body with conditions.times (includeAllTimes false, includeDays Mon-Fri 09:00-17:00 UTC) and the shape of includeRange / excludeRange found in the admin center's JavaScript.
articles.tested: Added the condition to a policy in Graph Explorer; the admin center then listed every condition as "Not configured".

articles.title: Logon Hours in Conditional Access
articles.says: Blocks sign-ins outside working hours with includeAllTimes true and excludeDays Mon-Fri 07:00-15:00 UTC; only "UTC" is accepted, "CET" returned an error.
articles.tested: PATCH returned 204; sign-ins tested 17-21/02/2026 - allowed 14:47 UTC, blocked 15:18 UTC, blocked on Saturday.

articles.title: Conditional Access Policies are the Best Way to Block Weekend Access to Microsoft 365
articles.says: Points to the time condition as an undocumented beta feature and argues a scheduled runbook that switches a block policy on and off does the same today.

articles.title: Access token lifetime
articles.says: Access tokens get a random lifetime of 60-90 minutes; Conditional Access is evaluated when a token is issued - why a session can outlive the time window.

articles.title: Continuous access evaluation - token lifetime
articles.says: With Continuous Access Evaluation, tokens can live up to 28 hours; revocation is driven by critical events, not by the clock.

uses: When documented: require extra checks before an agent performs a chosen action, not only when it signs in
Plan with the agent identities you already have - list them in Entra ID > Agent ID

articles.title: Conditional Access for agents

The page does not mention 'agent actions' or includeAgentActions.

conditionalAccessConditionSet|purviewDat.title: Conditional Access condition: Purview DLP rules
conditionalAccessConditionSet|purviewDat.what: A new condition linking Conditional Access with Microsoft Purview data loss prevention rules. Talk to the Purview team now - the condition needs DLP rules to exist

conditionalAccessSessionControls|network.title: Conditional Access session control: Global Secure Access profile (legacy)
conditionalAccessSessionControls|network.what: An older, undocumented twin of the documented session control globalSecureAccessFilteringProfile: it links a Conditional Access policy to a Global Secure Access security profile with policyId and isEnabled, and carries the same profile id. Microsoft's own GSA tools (Migrate2GSA, GSA-Policy-Workbench) read it but call it legacy and not a documented contract.
uses: Use the documented globalSecureAccessFilteringProfile (profileId, isEnabled) to link a security profile - not this one
When you export or migrate policies, read both: older policies may carry only this one
Do not build automation that writes it - Microsoft's own tool says not to build guidance on it
